That is a defined, citeable set; it is not the same as “everyone Gatorade has ever paid or might still use in archival footage.”

### College basketball and NIL (reporting-backed sequence)
Gatorade’s NCAA basketball NIL story, as reported in the trades, follows a clear order:
*   **Paige Bueckers** — described as the first college athlete to sign with Gatorade.  
*   **Caitlin Clark** — signed while at Iowa; the brand relationship continued after she turned pro.  
*   **JuJu Watkins** — joined the elite roster as the **third** NCAA women’s basketball NIL signing after Bueckers and Clark.  
*   **Cooper Flagg** — the **first men’s** NCAA basketball player to sign with Gatorade.
Those details matter for anyone comparing Gatorade to volume-first college strategies: the brand often picks nationally known names early, not a long tail of roster filler. Partnerships still imply product usage, content duties, and category exclusivity clauses where negotiated.

### Legacy and global: “GOAT Camp”
Gatorade has grouped **Michael Jordan**, **Serena Williams**, **Lionel Messi**, and **Usain Bolt** in its global “GOAT Camp” push—a useful anchor for “all-time face of the brand” talent even when day-to-day campaign rotation changes.

### Other notable past or reported names (not a current roster)
Trade and campaign coverage have also tied Gatorade to names such as **Mia Hamm**, **Abby Wambach**, **Jayson Tatum**, **Karl-Anthony Towns**, **Peyton Manning**, **Eli Manning**, **Dwyane Wade**, **Derek Jeter**, and **J.J. Watt**, alongside figures already listed above (e.g. **Candace Parker**). Treat these as **legacy, regional, or campaign-specific** unless a fresh release says otherwise—exactly because Gatorade does not publish one consolidated list.
College athlete deals more broadly took off after 2021 NIL rules, giving brands access to student-athletes before the pro draft. Gatorade’s public pattern has skewed toward hoops and other high-visibility sports when it wants headline density, not necessarily toward the longest possible tally of signings.

## Understanding Gatorade Player of the Year Awards
The Gatorade Player of the Year program recognizes elite high school athletes across 12 sports, functioning as both an awards system and a talent identification pipeline. Winners receive national recognition that often precedes professional success.
Each year, Gatorade selects 610 State Players of the Year across sports including football, basketball, baseball, soccer, and volleyball. From that pool, 12 National Players of the Year get chosen, one per sport. Selection criteria weigh athletic performance, academic achievement, and community involvement.
Past winners include Peyton Manning, LeBron James, Jayson Tatum, and Paige Bueckers. These athletes earned the recognition before college recruitment, giving them visibility when it matters most for scholarship offers. College coaches track Gatorade Player of the Year recipients as indicators of future performance and potential NIL value.

## Gatorade's NIL Deals With College Athletes
Gatorade entered college NIL partnerships by targeting athletes with existing national profiles: **Paige Bueckers** and **Caitlin Clark** before **JuJu Watkins** (third women’s NCAA basketball NIL in that sequence, as typically reported). Cooper Flagg became the brand's first men's college basketball NIL signee before his freshman season at Duke. Other college partnerships (for example **Shedeur Sanders** in football) show up in reporting but sit outside that basketball signing order.
The selection pattern is clear: Gatorade signs athletes who already carry recognition before college enrollment. Flagg arrived as the top-ranked recruit. Watkins broke freshman scoring records. This approach differs from brands spreading NIL budgets across hundreds of athletes. Gatorade picks fewer partners but invests in those positioned to dominate headlines throughout their college careers, using different strategies than NIL platforms.

## Notable Gatorade Football Players and Endorsement Deals
Public football storytelling from Gatorade often blends **NFL-adjacent campaigns** (specific players vary by year and are best verified per release) with **non-tackle growth bets**. **Diana Flores** is the clearest documented example on the 2026 “Body of Science” roster: flag football ahead of the sport’s **2028 Olympic** moment, paired with hydration messaging that fits training and recovery content. When you see NFL names in Gatorade creative, check the **press footnote for that campaign** rather than assuming they remain on an evergreen “roster page”—because Gatorade does not maintain one.

## Gatorade Basketball Stars and Brand Ambassadors
Michael Jordan's partnership with Gatorade produced the "Be Like Mike" campaign in 1991, creating the blueprint for how sports drinks connect product use to performance outcomes. That relationship ran for decades and made basketball central to Gatorade's brand strategy; he also appears in the later **GOAT Camp** framing alongside Serena Williams, Lionel Messi, and Usain Bolt.
On the men’s side, **reporting and past campaigns** have linked Gatorade to stars such as **Jayson Tatum** and **Karl-Anthony Towns**; treat any **current** NBA list as provisional unless tied to a dated announcement. Women’s basketball is easier to lock to 2026 source material: **Caitlin Clark**, **Paige Bueckers**, **JuJu Watkins**, **A’ja Wilson**, **Candace Parker**, and **Sophia Wilson** all appear on the **Body of Science** named list above, spanning college, WNBA, and national-team contexts.
Gatorade's women's portfolio in **announced 2026 creative** spans basketball, track, soccer, flag football, and motorsports: **Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone**, **Mallory Swanson**, **Diana Flores**, and **Lisa Billard** tie the brand to Olympic and Olympic-path disciplines alongside the hoops names on the Body of Science list. **Serena Williams** remains the anchor example for tennis and long-tail brand history, including **GOAT Camp**; other soccer or USWNT names may surface in **tournament-timed** campaigns—again, verify per release rather than assuming a static roster.
Lisa Billard's F1 Academy alignment follows the same early-investment story as flag football: show up before the category is saturated, pair credibly with performance and recovery, and own a lane while audiences are still scaling.
Each sport requires different hydration protocols. Tennis demands different electrolyte ratios than soccer. Recovery windows shift between racing and team sports. These variations create content where athletes explain training specifics, turning product use into educational material that runs on social channels year-round.

Segment Overview  
Information regarding our use of AOI to evaluate the performance of our operating segments can be found in Part II —Financial Information —Item 8.—Financial Statements and Supplementary Data—Note 12 –  
Segments and Revenue Recognition.  
Concerts  
Revenue and related costs for events are generally deferred and recognized when the event occurs. All advertising costs incurred during the year for shows in future years are expensed at the end of the year. If a  
current year event is rescheduled into a future year, all advertising costs incurred to date are expensed in the period when the event is rescheduled.  
Concerts direct operating expenses include artist fees, event production costs, show-related marketing and advertising expenses, along with other costs.  
To judge the health of our Concerts segment, we primarily monitor the number of confirmed events and fan attendance in our network of owned or operated and third-party venues, talent fees, average paid  
attendance, market ticket pricing, advance ticket sales and the number of major artist clients under management. In addition, at our owned or operated venues and festivals, we monitor ancillary revenue per fan and  
premium ticket sales. For business that is conducted in foreign markets, we also compare the operating results from our foreign operations to prior periods without the impact of changes in foreign exchange rates.  
Ticketing  
Revenue related to ticketing service charges is recognized when the ticket is sold for our third-party clients. For our own events, where our concert promoters control ticketing, revenue is deferred and recognized  
when the event occurs. GTV represents the total amount of the transaction related to a ticket sale and includes the face value of the ticket as well as the service charge. We use GTV to evaluate changes in ticket fee revenue  
that are driven by the pricing of our service charges.  
Ticketing direct operating expenses include call center costs and credit card fees, along with other costs.
